Most RAG systems fail quietly: retrieval gets slightly worse, answers get slightly less grounded,
and nothing errors. This lab builds the pipeline *and* the instrument that would catch that —
structure-aware chunking, lexical and vector retrieval fused by rank, a reranking stage, a
groundedness check, and an evaluation harness reporting precision@k, recall@k, and MRR over a
labeled query set.

Source: [`labs/hybrid-retrieval`](https://github.com/vins13pattar/principal-ai-engineer-handbook/tree/main/labs/hybrid-retrieval)

<Aside type="caution" title="production-shaped, not production-ready">
  The pipeline, fusion, reranking, and evaluation harness are real and tested. The embedding
  function is deterministic feature hashing, not a model — see
  [What the hashing trick does not demonstrate](#what-the-hashing-trick-does-not-demonstrate), which
  is the most important thing to understand before drawing any conclusion from this lab's retrieval
  results.
</Aside>

## Retrieval pipeline

<Mermaid code={retrievalPipeline} title="Two retrievers, fused by rank, reranked, then measured" />

## What it demonstrates

- **Structure-aware chunking.** Chunks respect section headings and never split a paragraph unless
  that paragraph alone exceeds the size budget, with overlap carried across boundaries *within* a
  section. Chunking on a fixed character count is the most common way to make retrieval quietly bad.
- **Real BM25, not a keyword filter.** Okapi BM25 with IDF computed over the actual corpus, so
  lexical ranking reflects term rarity rather than raw frequency.
- **Rank fusion, not score averaging.** Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines the two rankings by
  *position*. BM25 scores and cosine similarities live on incomparable scales; averaging them
  directly produces a number with no meaning, dominated by whichever scale happens to be larger.
- **Reranking scoped to the fused candidate set.** Only the fused candidates are rescored, which is
  what makes a more expensive scoring function affordable.
- **Groundedness as a retrieval property.** The checker flags citations pointing at chunks the
  retriever never returned — catching the failure where an answer cites something plausible that was
  never actually retrieved.
- **Measurement, not vibes.** precision@k, recall@k, and MRR over a labeled set, so a change to
  chunking or fusion produces a number that moved rather than an impression.

## Why fuse by rank instead of averaging scores

This is the design decision most worth internalizing. A BM25 score is an unbounded sum of IDF-weighted
term contributions; a cosine similarity is bounded in `[-1, 1]`. They are not merely on different
*scales* — they are different *kinds* of quantity, and no fixed normalization makes them
commensurable across queries, because BM25's range shifts with query length and corpus statistics
while cosine's does not.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion sidesteps the problem entirely by discarding magnitudes and using only
position: a document ranked second by both retrievers scores the same regardless of whether its BM25
score was 4 or 400. That throws away real information, which is a genuine cost — but it buys a
combination that behaves consistently across queries, which score averaging does not.

<Aside type="tip" title="Interview signal">
  "Normalize both scores and take a weighted average" is the intuitive answer and it is subtly
  wrong. Being able to say *why* — that the two distributions shift independently with query and
  corpus, so a fixed normalization is only valid for one query — separates a considered answer from
  a remembered one.
</Aside>

## What the hashing trick does not demonstrate

The embedding function is deterministic feature hashing. It exercises the vector-retrieval path,
makes every test reproducible without API keys or ML dependencies, and keeps fusion honest because
its two inputs really are different ranking signals.

It does **not** provide semantic similarity. Hashed features match on shared tokens, so a query and
a chunk expressing the same idea in different words score near zero. No result from this lab
supports a claim like "vector search retrieved the paraphrase" — it cannot.

That limitation is why the evaluation harness is the most transferable part of the lab. Swapping in
a real embedding model should visibly move precision and recall on the labeled set. If it does not,
the problem is somewhere else in the pipeline, and you now have the instrument to find out where.

## Run it

```bash
cd labs/hybrid-retrieval
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e '.[dev]'
uvicorn retrieval.app:app --reload
```

The app preloads a small demo corpus (four documents, two headed sections each) and a matching
eight-case labeled evaluation set.

```bash
# Hybrid search
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/v1/search \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query": "how long are logs retained", "k": 3}'

# Run the labeled evaluation set: precision@k, recall@k, MRR
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/v1/evaluate
```

Change the chunk size or disable reranking, re-run `/v1/evaluate`, and watch the metrics move —
that loop is the point of the lab.

## Verify it

```bash
pytest      # 43 tests
ruff check .
mypy src
```

## Principal-level discussion points

1. Chunking is a retrieval decision, not a preprocessing detail. Splitting mid-paragraph or ignoring
   section structure degrades every downstream stage, and does so invisibly.
2. Rank fusion beats score fusion when the underlying scores are incommensurable — which, for
   lexical and vector retrieval, they always are.
3. Reranking is affordable precisely because it runs on a small fused candidate set. A reranker
   applied to the whole corpus is just an expensive retriever.
4. Groundedness checking belongs at the retrieval boundary: an answer citing a chunk that was never
   retrieved is a detectable failure, and detecting it does not require a model.
5. Without a labeled set and metrics, "we improved retrieval" is unfalsifiable. The evaluation
   harness is what converts RAG work from tuning-by-impression into engineering.
